overview: Fungi come in two basic growth forms, and telling them apart at a glance is the first skill in mycology.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Unicellular fungi that typically reproduce by budding, forming smooth, creamy colonies.
aspects.valueB: Multicellular fungi that grow as branching filaments (hyphae), forming fuzzy or powdery colonies.

aspects.label: Cellular Organization
aspects.valueB: Filamentous hyphae that intertwine into a mycelium.

aspects.label: Reproduction
aspects.valueA: Asexual budding (blastoconidia); some also form pseudohyphae under stress.
aspects.valueB: Asexual spore formation (conidia, sporangiospores) at specialized structures on the hyphae.

aspects.label: Colony Appearance
aspects.valueA: Smooth, moist, opaque colonies resembling bacterial colonies macroscopically.
aspects.valueB: Fuzzy, cottony, woolly, or powdery colonies, often pigmented.

aspects.label: Growth Behavior
aspects.valueA: Grow well at both room temperature and 37°C; some are dimorphic and switch forms with temperature.
aspects.valueB: Typically grow best at room temperature; some dimorphic fungi convert to a yeast form at 37°C in tissue.

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueA: Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
aspects.valueB: Aspergillus niger, Rhizopus species, dermatophytes like Trichophyton.

aspects.label: Laboratory Identification
aspects.valueA: Germ tube test, sugar fermentation/assimilation panels, chromogenic agar.
aspects.valueB: Lactophenol cotton blue mount to visualize hyphae and spore structures under the microscope.
